newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court says employee may sue in established workplace.
newsitem.headline: Court says employee may sue in established workplace.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday employees under contract may file suit against employers in the member state where their established centre of work lies.
A Dutch resident who was under contract with a British company and did business in Britain, the United States, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands filed suit against his employer in the Netherlands.

The British employer, Cross Medical Ltd, challenged the court's jurisdiction under the Brussels Convention. The court said when an employee carries out work in more than one country party to the Convention, jurisdiction lies with the courts in the place where work is "habitually" carried out.

The court said "habitually" referred to the place where the employee principally discharges responsibilities to the employer. Other criteria include the amount of time spent in one member state, where an office is maintained for organising activities and where the employee returns after traveling abroad.

The court also noted the Convention protects employees, considered in a weaker position than employers, and toward that end seeks to place jurisdiction where it is least expensive for the employee to begin, or defend against, court proceedings.

"The Brussels Convention cannot be interpreted as conferring concurrent jurisdiction on the courts of each contracting state in whose territory the employee performed part of his work," the court said.
The court said amendments to the Brussels Convention, known as the San Sebastian Convention, did not alter their interpretation of earlier case law in this area.
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: Dutch)

"Brussels Convention - Article 5(1) - Courts for the place of performance of the contractual obligation - Contract of employment - Place where the employee habitually carries out his work - Work performed in more than one country"
Reference from the Hoge Raad der Nederlanden for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings pending before that court between
on the interpretation of the Brussels Convention of 27 September 1968, as amended (OJ 1972 L 304, p. 1),

The Brussels Convention of 27 September 1968, as amended, must be interpreted as meaning that where, in the performance of a contract of employment, an employee carries out his work in several contracting states, the place where he habitually carries out his work, within the meaning of that provision, is the place wher he has established the effective centre of his working activities. When identifying that place, it is necessary to take into account the fact that the employee spends most of his working time in one of the contracting states in which he has an office where he organizes his activities for his employer and to which he returns after each business trip abroad.
